Vinnytsya Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Vinnytska oblast, Ukraine

Not demolished. Vinnytsia's Jewish burial society (Chevra Kadisha) was established in 1654, remarkably early for this collection, though this cemetery itself is dated to 1727 by IAJGS. The city's Jewish community, first mentioned in 1532, survived the massacres of Khmelnytsky's Cossacks in 1648 and repeated Haidamak violence in the 1740s, growing to 11,689 people (40 percent of the population) by 1897 — making Vinnytsia the third-largest Jewish community in Podolia, after Kamianets-Podilskyi and Uman. Adolf Hitler sited his eastern-front field headquarters, the Führerhauptquartier Werwolf, near Vinnytsia at Stryzhavka, built in 1941–1942 during the German occupation; Einsatzgruppe C carried out atrocities in the region, and an estimated 28,000 to 35,000 Jews were deported from the Vinnytsia area, most of whom later died. A Jewish community of about 1,700 people remained in Vinnytsia as of 2001. The cemetery today holds a few hundred matzevot dating from the 19th century through the first half of the 20th.
